newsitem.title: FRANCE: Dusty wartime files led to Papon trial in France.
newsitem.headline: Dusty wartime files led to Papon trial in France.

text.p: Were it not for the chance finding of wartime files in a dusty French attic, Maurice Papon, ex-budget minister and holder of the Legion of Honour could have enjoyed a quiet retirement worthy of a career civil servant.

But almost 16 years after that discovery, the Supreme Court on Thursday ordered Papon to face charges of crimes against humanity for deporting 1,690 Jews, including 223 children, from Bordeaux in southwestern France.
Most were gassed to death in Auschwitz concentration camp.
For decades Papon, 87, embodied the loyal servant of the state, as a faithful lieutenant to General Charles de Gaulle and then as budget minister under president Valery Giscard d'Estaing.

Frustrated by the delaying tactics of successive governments, relatives of the deportees had to battle for years to have a court examine whether there should be a trial and what one lawyer branded "the cold calculation of a civil servant concerned, above all, about his career".

After law studies Papon started his career as a Foreign Ministry aide and moved to Bordeaux in 1942 as secretary-general of the local administration, a job including responsibility for all issues concerning Jews. He was 26 years old.
"I only executed orders," Papon said later of the lists, arrests and convoys he organised and which were documented in the archives found in an attic in 1981.
Asked by his peers why he had not thought of resigning, he answered: "My character prevented me from doing so. I have never deserted the ground on which I was placed to fight."
After the war, Papon said he had belonged to two underground Resistance groups since 1943. De Gaulle named him a prefect, a senior post representing the state at departmental level.

His post-war rise was impressive, with appointments as chief administrator of Corsica and then secretary general of the Moroccan protectorate. He was elected Gaullist deputy in June 1968 and re-elected in 1973.

His tenure as Paris police chief in 1958-67 was marked by Arab riots in October 1961 during which beatings carried out by police under his orders resulted in dozens of Algerian bodies being fished out of the River Seine.
When the documents implicating him in war crimes appeared in the weekly "Le Canard Enchaine" in May 1981, then-budget minister Papon claimed he was being set up by leftists on the eve of elections.
He called for a jury of honour made up of five former Resistance members to attempt to show he had used his position to inform Resistance networks of police activity.

The special jury's conclusion, rendered in December 1981 was ambiguous, saying that Papon "contributed to certain acts that did not conform with the jury's concept of honour" and should have resigned from his official duties in 1942.
But it added that he had tried to help certain Jews and concluded charges against him were unjustified. In January 1983 Papon was indicted on charges of "crimes against humanity".
Lawyers seeking to bring Papon to book accused successive governments of delaying tactics to avoid the embarrassment of a trial that could dredge up damaging and painful memories.
In 1991 Papon told a news conference he was tired of being hounded by accusations and wanted to go to trial.
